findings.finding: THE SHIPPING TICKER RUNS IN NO TEST. Every test in this class injects ManualTicker through the 5-arg start; nothing exercises the 4-arg start's default ticker at LocalSequencer.java:141-147 -- which is the only overload DefaultIngest calls. SURVIVING MUTATION, measured in a copy of the staged tree: `sleepFor(leases.renewInterval())` -> `sleepFor(java.time.Duration.ofDays(1))`. Full `./gradlew test` BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 1m49-1m54s, zero failures. So the task's whole criterion -- a healthy leader renews BEFORE its TTL -- is asserted only against a ticker the test supplies, and a production ticker wired to the wrong duration (or to none) is green. This is the identical defect the sibling seam already fixed and documented: BatchingSequencerTest.java:267-306 (`theRealClockTimerActuallyWaitsItsInterval`) opens with 'THE SHIPPING TIMER RAN IN NO TEST ... `() -> Thread.sleep(millis)` could have been a no-op and criterion 9 would still read green', and records `sleepFor(interval)` -> `sleepFor(interval.multipliedBy(4))` and a constant-sleep timer as mutations a lower bound alone did not kill. LocalSequencer follows that seam but not its test. Cheap kill of the same shape: one T1 test through the 4-arg start with a short legal renewInterval (LeaseConfig only requires 0 < renewInterval < ttl, so e.g. ttl=2s/renew=300ms), bounded on BOTH sides on the stored lease expiry -- a lower bound alone is met by a ticker that ignores its argument, an upper bound alone by one that never waits. Note also that LocalSequencer.sleepFor is `private static` where BatchingSequencer.sleepFor is package-private precisely so it can be pinned directly.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.17 ships and the lease is still not renewed in production. `leases.renewInterval()` is replaced by `ttl`, by a constant, or by a future refactor that drops the argument, and every test in this class keeps passing because they all hand in their own ticker. The cluster keeps failing over at each TTL and burning an epoch per failover -- the exact liveness defect this row exists to close, plus the M4.16 compounding it names -- with a green suite and a backlog row marked done. Nothing downstream would find it: coverage sees `sleepFor` executed at construction, and the only assertion about renew timing lives on a code path production never takes.

findings.finding: Nothing constrains HOW MANY store requests one tick costs. aHealthyLeaderRENEWSSoItsTermDoesNotLapse uses a bare MemoryBinStore and asserts only that the stored expiry moved, so any number of renews per tick satisfies it. SURVIVING MUTATION, measured: insert two extra `leases.renew();` calls before the guarded one in renewForever (LocalSequencer.java:92) -- three lease putIfMatch per tick instead of one. `./gradlew :sequencer:test :ingest:test` BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 25s. The fixture to kill it is already used two tests down: wrap the store in CountingBinStore (as the fenced test does at :167) and assert the tick costs exactly one put. That also makes the healthy-leader test a cost assertion rather than only a liveness one, which testing.md rule 22 asks for and which is the dimension this project exists to control.
findings.failure_scenario: A retry loop, a duplicated call, or a refresh-then-renew added inside renewForever multiplies the lease's PUT rate per pod per interval, and no test notices -- LeaseManager's own comment ('A read per renew would double the lease's request rate for nothing') is the concern, one layer down, with no assertion at the layer that now drives it.

findings.finding: `Thread.sleep(50)` is a fixed sleep used to SYNCHRONISE, which testing.md rule 15 forbids outright and which this module argues against in its own fixtures (BatchingSequencerTest.java:57-62, 'a BOUNDED POLL, not the fixed sleep testing.md forbids ... No test in this class sleeps to synchronise'; LeaseManagerConcurrencyTest.java:234, 'Bounded spin, never Thread.sleep -- testing.md leaves no escape'). It is the only thing that makes the `seq.commit` at :237 non-vacuous: measured by deleting it in a copy of the tree, the fence-on-IOException mutation is STILL killed, but by awaitExpiryPast at :247 after its full 20-second deadline, not by the commit. So the commit assertion is a race, not a rendezvous, and the mutations it alone would catch survive whenever 50ms is not enough on a loaded machine -- e.g. a transient `renewFailing` flag set in the IOException catch and cleared on the next successful renew, which commitAll refuses on: with the window lost, the commit precedes the failed renew, the flag is cleared before the assertion, and the mutant is green. Wait on an observable instead (a counter FailPutIfMatchStore increments on the injected throw). The two polls at :123 and :203 are NOT this: both re-read a real observable under a 20s deadline and fail loudly, which is the QueuedTimer pattern -- though neither carries the one-line argument the sibling insists on.
findings.failure_scenario: CI or a WSL2 session under load delays the renewer past 50ms. The commit at :237 then runs before the failing renew is even attempted, and the test reports 'a store failure does not fence a healthy leader' having never observed a store failure reach the renewer. The assertion is not flaky-red -- it is silently vacuous, which is worse, because the half that still works (the recover-and-renew-again half) keeps the test green.

findings.finding: close() versus the renewer is untested in both directions. TWO SURVIVING MUTATIONS, applied together, measured: (a) delete `renewer.interrupt();` in close(), and (b) delete the post-tick `if (closed) { return; }` at LocalSequencer.java:89-91. Full `./gradlew test` BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 1m49s. (a) is the only mechanism that stops the renewer promptly, and with an injected ticker that never fires again it leaves the virtual thread parked for the JVM's lifetime; (b) is the guard that stops a tick delivered concurrently with close() from calling leases.renew() around leases.release(), whose observable is exactly the distinction the field's javadoc (LocalSequencer.java:64-74) says must be preserved -- a normal shutdown must report CLOSED, never 'lost its lease ... has been fenced'. The seam already present makes it cheap: close(), then tick(), then assert the commit refusal names the shutdown rather than a takeover, and that the renewer is no longer alive. Related hazard class is already filed as M4.35 for BatchingSequencer's committer.
findings.failure_scenario: A tick lands while close() is between `closed = true` and `leases.release()`. The renewer renews a lease the shutdown is about to expire, or reads back empty after the release and sets `fenced`, so the next caller and the log both report that this node was FENCED by a takeover when it was shut down deliberately -- an operator chases a failover that never happened. Alternatively the interrupt is dropped in a refactor as redundant and every closed sequencer leaks a parked renewer thread. Nothing in the suite moves in either case.
